paragraphs: Once the legislative power is well established, the next thing is to establish the executive power in the same way; for the executive power, which operates only by particular acts and is not of the essence of the legislative power, is naturally separate from it. If it were possible for the Sovereign, as such, to hold the executive power, right and fact would be so confused that no one could tell what was law and what was not; and the body politic, thus disfigured, would soon fall prey to the very violence it was instituted to prevent.

Since the citizens are all equal by the social compact, all can prescribe what all should do, but no one has a right to demand that another do what he does not do himself. It is strictly this right, which is indispensable for giving the body politic life and movement, that the Sovereign confers upon the prince when it institutes the government.

It has been held that this act of establishment was a contract between the people and the rulers it sets over itself — a contract laying down conditions between the two parties, binding the one to command and the other to obey. It will be admitted, I am sure, that this is an odd kind of contract to enter into. But let us see whether this view can be upheld.

First, the supreme authority can no more be modified than it can be given away; to limit it is to destroy it. It is absurd and self-contradictory for the Sovereign to set a superior over itself; to bind itself to obey a master would be to return to absolute liberty.

Moreover, it is clear that this contract between the people and such and such persons would be a particular act; and it follows that it can be neither a law nor an act of Sovereignty, and that it would consequently be illegitimate.

It is plain, too, that the contracting parties would be under the law of nature alone in relation to each other, with no guarantees of their mutual undertakings at all, a position wholly at odds with the civil state. Whoever has force at his command is always in a position to control the carrying out of the contract, so it would come to the same thing if the name “contract” were given to the act of one man who said to another, “I give you all my goods, on condition that you give me back as much of them as you please.”

There is only one contract in the State, and that is the act of association, which by itself excludes any second contract. It is impossible to conceive of any public contract that would not violate the first.
